notes: "His face was not pretty." reads slightly odd for a male figure; "His face was not nice to look at." or "He was not handsome." would be more natural, but A1 readers will not stumble.
Here Fritz gives the sword directly to the Nutcracker, while other levels route it through Marie. This is an acceptable simplification and does not contradict them.
Grammar stays in present and past simple throughout. The Hard Nut back-story is compressed cleanly and stays faithful.
"Later, Marie whispered..." followed by "That afternoon..." works, though "That same afternoon" would make the timing a little clearer.

"Soon the big clock struck twelve. Hundreds of mice were coming out from the cracks in the floor." The sudden past continuous is a little flat; "Hundreds of mice came running out of the cracks in the floor." reads better.
No conditionals or passives found. "Give me your sweets, or I will bite your Nutcracker" is imperative + or, which is fine at B1.

In the Hard Nut tale the young man is only 'the king's clockmaker's own nephew'. Unlike A2, B1 and C1, this level never says the clockmaker was a Drosselmeier, so the link to Godfather Drosselmeier's nephew is left for the reader to infer. Adding "the king's clockmaker, who was also called Drosselmeier," would close it.

"'If you were real, I would never laugh at you like that princess did.' 'I would love you just as you are,' she added." Two back-to-back quotes from the same speaker read a little choppily and could be merged into one quotation.

"Godfather Drosselmeier picked them up with a curious smile..." Drosselmeier's presence at the breakfast scene is never set up. "Godfather Drosselmeier, who had dropped in that morning, picked them up..." would smooth it.

Strong fidelity: glass wig, owl with Drosselmeier's face, sugar-plum cannons, the bacon and sausage origin of the curse, the unshaven, bootless youth, the steps backwards, the astronomer's prophecy, the watch-chain explanation, the father's coat sleeve, and the sisters at the Marzipan Castle.

summary: All five levels give a faithful, child-safe retelling of Hoffmann's tale (not the ballet or film versions) with a consistent plot across levels, grammar suited to each level, and correctly keyed quizzes. The only remaining points are minor polish items: a missing clockmaker-Drosselmeier link at B2, Drosselmeier's unexplained presence at C1's breakfast, and a flat past continuous at B1.
